chapters.title: Chapter 2: Detecting Regimes: From Rules to Statistics

lessons.title: Rolling Volatility and Drawdown as Regime Signals

body.text: India VIX tells you what the options market expects. Rolling realized volatility and drawdown tell you what the price series has actually done, no options data required, and they disagree with VIX often enough to matter.

children.text: The previous lesson leaned on India VIX for the volatility dimension. That is convenient, but India VIX only exists back to April 2008 and only exists for the index, not for individual stocks or other markets you might trade. Realized volatility, computed directly from a return series, has no such limits: it works on any instrument with a price history. This lesson builds it, along with a second, closely related signal, drawdown, that price data alone can give you.
Rolling Realized Volatility, Computed From Returns

Chapter 1 defined realized volatility as the annualized standard deviation of daily returns. Turning that into a regime signal just means computing it on a rolling window instead of once over a fixed period, so it updates every day as new returns arrive.

body.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

nifty_df['daily_return'] = nifty_df['close'].pct_change()
nifty_df['realized_vol_20d'] = (
    nifty_df['daily_return'].rolling(window=20).std() * np.sqrt(252)
)
body.caption: 20-day rolling realized volatility, annualized

children.text: Realized volatility is symmetric by construction: a sharp 3% rally and a sharp 3% selloff contribute the same amount to the standard deviation. From a pure statistics standpoint that is correct. From a risk management standpoint it can be misleading, because a portfolio manager does not lose sleep over volatility on the upside. That gap is exactly what drawdown is built to capture.

Drawdown measures how far the current price sits below the highest price seen so far: the running maximum. It is always zero or negative, it resets to zero every time a new high is made, and unlike realized volatility it only reacts to declines. Two markets can post identical realized volatility over a month, one grinding sideways with large two-way swings and one falling in a straight line, and drawdown tells them apart instantly while realized volatility alone cannot.

body.caption: Drawdown from the running peak, as a fraction (e.g. -0.17 for a 17% drawdown)

body.title: Illustrative: Nifty 50 Rolling Drawdown From Running Peak, Q4 2019 to Q4 2022

body.text: The drawdown path above is a rounded, illustrative reconstruction consistent with the peak-to-trough figures used earlier in this course (roughly 38% in the 2020 COVID crash, roughly 17% in the 2022 correction), not an exact tick-by-tick series.

children.text: The shape above does what a single trend flag from the previous lesson cannot: it shows the depth of the 2020 and 2022 drawdowns on the same axis, at a glance. The 2020 line falls almost three times as far as the 2022 line, a difference the earlier binary trend_flag would show as identically 'down' in both cases.
Reading Drawdown Depth and Volatility Together

Drawdown depth alone is not enough either. A 10% drawdown that develops over six calm months and a 10% drawdown that develops in six violent days are very different regimes even though the number is identical. Pairing drawdown depth with the realized volatility (or India VIX) reading at the same time produces a sharper classification than either signal alone.

body.text: Notice that the boundary between 'Correction' and 'Deep Correction' is a judgment call, not a law of markets, exactly like the India VIX bands in the previous lesson. You are still drawing hard lines through continuous numbers. The lines are more informative now, because two signals are voting instead of one, but they have not stopped being arbitrary lines.

children.text: That is the theme the next lesson takes head on. Every rule-based signal built so far, trend flags, India VIX bands, realized volatility, and drawdown, shares the same DNA: pick a window, pick a threshold, and label whatever crosses it. Lesson 3 measures exactly how much that costs in whipsawed regime labels and shows why the thresholds themselves resist being chosen in any principled way.

body.title: Computing a Drawdown
body.prompt: Nifty's running peak so far this year is 26,000. It closes today at 22,880. What is today's drawdown, as a percentage (enter as a positive number, e.g. 12 for a 12% drawdown)?
body.explanation: Drawdown = (close / running_max) - 1 = (22880 / 26000) - 1 = -0.12, or a 12% drawdown. The sign is dropped here only because the exercise asked for magnitude; in code, keep it as a negative number so it composes correctly with other signals.

body.title: Same Drawdown, Different Regime
body.scenario: Two Nifty drawdowns both bottom out at exactly -14%. Drawdown A develops over 5 trading sessions with realized 20-day volatility rising from 14% to 42% along the way. Drawdown B develops over 4 months with realized 20-day volatility staying in a 13% to 17% range throughout.
body.prompt: Using the drawdown-and-volatility table from this lesson, which regime label fits each drawdown, and what would you expect to be different about how a systematic desk should respond to each?
body.modelAnswer: Drawdown A, a 14% fall in 5 sessions with realized volatility roughly tripling, fits Deep Correction or Emerging Risk-Off Regime, closer in character to the 2022 episode but compressed into days rather than months, and the sharp volatility spike is itself informative. A desk should treat this as a fast-developing regime shift, cut directional risk quickly, and expect further whipsaws while volatility remains elevated. Drawdown B, the same 14% fall spread across 4 calm months with volatility barely moving, looks more like a slow, orderly Correction. It does not carry the same urgency; a desk can afford to wait for more confirmation before treating it as a full regime change, since drawdown depth without a volatility signature is weaker evidence on its own.

points: Realized volatility, computed from returns, works on any price series with history, unlike India VIX which only exists back to 2008 and only for the index
Realized volatility is symmetric between up and down moves; drawdown is not, and captures the distance from a running peak specifically
Drawdown resets to zero at every new high and only accumulates on declines, making it a direction-aware complement to a symmetric volatility measure
Pairing drawdown depth with a volatility reading produces a sharper regime classification than either signal alone
The thresholds used to bucket drawdown depth and volatility remain judgment calls, not laws of markets, which is the limitation the next lesson measures directly
